title: Rivers in the Sky Are Soaking the Pacific Northwest
summary:
It's the wettest time of the year in one of the wettest parts of the country: the Pacific Northwest. This week, heavy rain, high tides, and rising sea levels are hitting the West Coast. Two atmospheric rivers will pound parts of Oregon and Washington on Friday and Saturday, after two others already dropped inches of rain on both states earlier this week.

So what is an atmospheric river? Think of it as a river in the sky: a narrow band of water vapor pushed along by the wind. It dumps rain or snow over a wide area. These rivers can stretch up to 2,000 miles long and 600 miles wide, said F. Martin Ralph, a researcher at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

Atmospheric rivers are a natural climate pattern. About 50 to 60 percent of California's rain comes from them, said Josh Weiss, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The season runs from October to March, and this year it is off to a fast start.

The trouble comes when several rivers arrive one after another. 'What's really problematic is when you get compounding impacts from multiple atmospheric rivers,' Weiss said — flash flooding, urban flooding, and even landslides. Washington's coast could see 20-foot swells this weekend, said Jeff Michalski of the National Weather Service in Seattle.

Right now, the rivers are arriving with El Niño's warm ocean waters and the year's highest tides, called king tides, putting coastal and inland waterways at risk of flooding. People may know atmospheric rivers by nicknames like Pineapple Express, which describe where the river begins. Forty years of data from the Federal Emergency Management Agency show that 90 percent or more of all flood damage in the Western U.S. comes from atmospheric rivers.
why_it_matters: Atmospheric rivers bring much of the West Coast's rain, but when several arrive at once they can cause flooding and landslides that damage homes and communities. Understanding them helps people prepare for the risks that come with the rain they depend on.

background_read: An atmospheric river is a narrow band of moist air that flows through the sky like a river, carrying huge amounts of water vapor from the ocean toward land.
Wind pushes this band along, and when it reaches land and rises over mountains or meets cooler air, the water vapor cools and falls as rain or snow.
These rivers are a natural part of the weather, and they bring much of the rain that fills rivers and reservoirs along the West Coast.
Problems start when several of them arrive one after another, because the ground is already soaked and the extra water has nowhere to go, which can cause flooding and landslides.
